claims.statement: Liraglutide is a synthetic glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist analog used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, prevention of cardiovascular complications associated with diabetes, and obesity.

extractedEvidence.quote: Liraglutide is a GLP-1 analog used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, prevention of cardiovascular complications associated with diabetes, and obesity.

claims.statement: The FDA-approved Victoza (liraglutide) label states it is indicated (1) as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus, and (2) to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease.

context.population: adults and pediatric patients aged 10+ with type 2 diabetes; adults with T2D and established cardiovascular disease
context.useCase: approved indication — glycemic control / cardiovascular risk reduction in T2D

extractedEvidence.quote: as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus
to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease
The application received original approval on January 25, 2010, as a Type 1 - New Molecular Entity under standard review. Marketing Status: Prescription.

reviewFlags: regulatory approved-indication claim — confirm current label version at review time

Independent review 2026-08-29: content re-verified against the live, current FDA label PDF and corroborated against Drugs@FDA (structured-database family, distinct from the label document family) confirming active NDA approval and marketing status; wording matches verbatim. A professional-guideline family (e.g., ADA Standards of Care) was not additionally checked this session -- gap recorded in ops.reviewReasons.

claims.statement: The FDA-approved Saxenda (liraglutide 3 mg/day) label states it is indicated, in combination with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, to reduce excess body weight in (a) adults and pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with body weight above 60 kg and obesity, and (b) adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbid condition.

context.doseText: Label titration schedule: 0.6 mg/day week 1, 1.2 mg week 2, 1.8 mg week 3, 2.4 mg week 4, 3 mg maintenance from week 5 onward — label/protocol context, not a use recommendation.

claims.statement: Both Victoza and Saxenda (liraglutide) carry an FDA boxed warning that liraglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents at clinically relevant exposures, with human relevance undetermined; liraglutide is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2), and in patients with serious hypersensitivity to liraglutide or its excipients.

context.population: patients considering or using liraglutide products

Liraglutide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell tumors at clinically relevant exposures in both genders of rats and mice.

reviewFlags: verify current label text at review time — labels are periodically revised

Independent review 2026-08-29: boxed-warning text re-verified verbatim against live current FDA label PDFs (Victoza 2025 s046, Saxenda 2026 s025). claims.statement: The Victoza label documents reports of acute pancreatitis (including fatal and non-fatal hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis), gastrointestinal adverse reactions (sometimes severe), acute gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis/cholecystitis), increased hypoglycemia risk when combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue, and rare reports of pulmonary aspiration during elective surgery in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists.

extractedEvidence.quote: Acute pancreatitis, including fatal and non-fatal hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis, has been observed
Acute events of gallbladder disease such as cholelithiasis or cholecystitis have been reported
pulmonary aspiration in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists undergoing elective surgeries

reviewFlags: Independent literature review 2026-08-29 (Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine review of GLP-1 agonists and pancreatitis, https://www.ccjm.org/content/92/8/483) confirms the label's postmarketing-report basis for the pancreatitis warning, consistent with this claim's hedged 'documents reports of' framing. Nuance for balance: multiple meta-analyses cited in that review did not find a statistically significant class-wide increase in pancreatitis incidence versus comparators, and a Cleveland Clinic cohort found recurrence rates in patients with prior pancreatitis were not clearly elevated.

claims.statement: In the LEADER trial (liraglutide vs. placebo added to standard care in 9,340 adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk), the primary composite cardiovascular outcome (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke) occurred in fewer patients in the liraglutide group (608 of 4,668 patients, 13.0%) than in the placebo group (694 of 4,672 patients, 14.9%), hazard ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.78-0.97, p=0.01 for superiority); this trial underlies Victoza's cardiovascular risk-reduction indication.

context.population: adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk (n=9,340)
context.useCase: cardiovascular outcome reduction in type 2 diabetes
context.doseText: LEADER trial protocol dosing (Marso et al., 2016); trial context only, not a use recommendation.

extractedEvidence.quote: The primary composite outcome occurred in fewer patients in the liraglutide group (608 of 4668 patients [13.0%]) than in the placebo group (694 of 4672 [14.9%]) (hazard ratio, 0.87; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.78 to 0.97; P=0.01 for superiority).

reviewFlags: REMEDIATED 2026-08-29: prior figure (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.94, p=0.005) was misattributed from a post-MI subgroup analysis (PMC6130125) and has been replaced with the trial-wide primary composite outcome, verified verbatim against the primary Marso et al. NEJM 2016 publication (PMC4985288) fetched this session.

claims.statement: A CADTH clinical review of Saxenda's pivotal SCALE phase 3 trials found statistically significant placebo-adjusted body-weight reductions with liraglutide 3 mg, including a treatment difference of −5.39% (95% CI −5.82 to −4.95, p<0.0001) in the main trial (Study 1839), with odds of achieving ≥5% weight loss about 4.8-fold higher than placebo (OR 4.80, 95% CI 4.12–5.60, p<0.0001). The same review flagged evidence gaps: underrepresentation of patients with BMI 27 to <30 kg/m2, a lack of comparative (head-to-head) evidence, and trial populations that were predominantly White and female, limiting generalizability.

context.useCase: chronic weight management — efficacy evidence base
context.doseText: 3 mg/day maintenance per SCALE trial protocol and label titration; trial context only, not a use recommendation.

authority-support-pass 2026-08-29: added dailymed-saxenda-label (A1, regulator-label) as an independent authoritative source, fetched live this session, directly quoting the FDA-approved label's Clinical Studies section (14.1) reporting statistically significant placebo-adjusted weight loss from the SCALE trial program — corroborating this claim's overall finding of statistically significant weight-loss efficacy. Note: the label's Study 1 point estimates (LSMean difference -4.5%, 62.3% achieving ≥5% loss) differ numerically from the CADTH review's cited Study 1839 estimates (-5.39%, 62.3% vs different OR-based framing) due to different analysis populations/estimands reported by each source; both independently confirm statistical significance (p<0.0001) of liraglutide's weight-loss effect versus placebo, so the CADTH-sourced figures in this claim's statement are left unchanged and the label serves as corroborating, not replacement, evidence.

claims.statement: Illegal online sellers market GLP-1 agonist injectables — the drug class that includes liraglutide — without requiring a valid prescription, and some sellers evade enforcement by labeling products 'peptides' intended 'for research purposes only' and 'not for human consumption.' Substandard and falsified GLP-1 products have been identified in multiple countries. Separately, FDA states that compounded drug products are not FDA-approved and have not undergone FDA review for safety, effectiveness, or quality. No human outcome data support unsupervised, non-prescription self-administration of liraglutide-class products obtained through these channels, and such use falls outside any FDA-approved label.

context.population: consumers purchasing GLP-1 injectables online outside licensed pharmacy channels
context.formulation: unregulated / compounded / 'research-use' GLP-1 product marketed as or alongside liraglutide
context.useCase: marketing-versus-evidence gap for gray-market GLP-1 weight-loss products

extractedEvidence.quote: Criminals sell these drugs online without requiring a valid prescription and without the required pharmacy licenses.
try to skirt enforcement by advertising drugs as 'peptides' with claims that they are for 'research purposes only' and 'not for human consumption.'
substandard and falsified Ozempic® has been found in at least 16 countries to date
extractedEvidence.pageOrSection: Report summary, citing the Partnership for Safe Medicines

extractedEvidence.quote: Compounded drugs are not approved by FDA.

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: captures the marketing/evasion pattern for the GLP-1 injectable class broadly; the source's documented falsification example (Ozempic/semaglutide) is class-adjacent rather than liraglutide-specific — a liraglutide-specific falsification incident count was not confirmed this session
no approved indication supports non-prescription self-administration

Independent review 2026-08-29 (FDA counterfeit-Ozempic consumer warning, WHO fake-semaglutide alert, and a 2026 Frontiers in Pharmacology pharmacovigilance analysis) reconfirms the broader gray-market pattern but found every documented falsification/counterfeit incident across sources checked to be semaglutide/Ozempic-specific, not liraglutide-specific. The claim's class-level (not liraglutide-specific) framing is accurate and remains unchanged; gap stays open and review-gated.

conflicts.summary: LEADER trial primary composite-outcome figures were originally extracted via a secondary subgroup-analysis publication (PMC6130125) because the primary NEJM article (Marso et al., 2016;375:311-322) returned a bot-check page and was inaccessible during the initial research session. Independent re-fetch of the primary publication (PMC4985288) on 2026-08-29 shows the originally-cited figure (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.94, p=0.005) was a subgroup-specific statistic, not the trial-wide primary outcome. The claim has been corrected to the verified trial-wide result: HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.78-0.97), p=0.01 for superiority (13.0% liraglutide vs 14.9% placebo, n=9,340), quoted verbatim from PMC4985288.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

RESOLVED 2026-08-29: LEADER trial primary-outcome figure was corrected to HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.78-0.97, p=0.01 for superiority) after independently re-fetching and quoting the primary Marso et al. NEJM 2016 publication (PMC4985288); prior figure (HR 0.82) was a misattributed subgroup statistic.

RESOLVED 2026-08-29: CAS number (204656-20-2, via PubChem), UNII (839I73S42A, via FDA/NCATS GSRS), RxNorm RxCUI (475968, via RxNav), and ChEMBL ID (CHEMBL4084119, via ChEMBL API) were resolved and added to compound.externalIdentifiers this session.

A professional-guideline family (e.g., ADA Standards of Care) has not yet been consulted for these fieldAuthorityRequired claims; remains a documented gap pending further review.
